newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil says debate on privatization proceeds over.
newsitem.headline: Brazil says debate on privatization proceeds over.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's decision to assign all privatization proceeds to debt retirement ends a furious debate within the government between populists and fiscal disciplinarians, officials said.

Finance Minister Pedro Malan, in the United States for talks with International Monetary Fund officials and with economists, said the decision showed Brazil was capable of dealing with its fiscal woes, the Gazeta Mercantil financial daily reported.
"Our position is very clear," the paper Thursday quoted Malan as saying.

"The receipts must be used to reduce the public debt stock. The reasons are known and this demonstrates that we are capable of dealing with Brazil's fiscal problems in the medium and long term," he said.

The issue of what to do with money raised from state sell-offs has long pitted the "technocrats" in the government's economics team against the politicians who want to see more social investment ahead of next year's presidential elections.
The argument heated up dramatically Tuesday when outspoken Communications Minister Sergio Motta criticized the Central Bank for favouring economic stability above economic development.

His off-the-cuff comments, which suggested a split in the government over policy but which he later denied making, fuelled an already-plunging stock market, nervous about rumors of a possible Brazilian devaluation in the slipstream of Asian currency woes.

But officials said President Cardoso decided Tuesday night in a meeting with ministers to brave congressional pressure for budget largesse and underline his government's commitment to getting its finances in order.
"All of the money raised through privatizations as well as concessions will be used to reduce public debt," Presidential spokesman Sergio Amaral said.
Amaral made clear, however, that even though the government had closed the door on using sell-offs to fund social projects, it had not locked it.

No one was considering, "for the moment", using privatization receipts to pay for social projects, Amaral said, declining to rule out the possibility of a change of heart as the October 1998 polls come closer.
Under Brazil's National Privatization Program, privatization funds have automatically been earmarked for debt, officials say.

But that tradition was broken earlier this year with mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD), when half of the proceeds of the $3.0 billion sale of a controlling stake was ploughed into a special Economic Reconstruction Fund.
Some uncertainty also clouded the auction of concessions to run public services, such as the billion-dollar tenders to run B Band cellular services throughout Brazil.
Those concessions do not formally come under the privatization program.

But Amaral said the concession fees were also destined for reducing Brazil's monstrous net public sector debt stock, currently standing at about 280 billion reais, or 34 percent of gross domestic product.
Despite the current focus on Brazil's external accounts, analysts say it is in the fiscal area that the challenge lies.
Brazil posted a consolidated public sector operational deficit last year of 3.86 percent of GDP, expected to narrow this year to 3.16 percent of GDP, according to a Reuters survey.
